newsitem.title: UK: Weather sets tone as holiday subdues Europe grains.
newsitem.headline: Weather sets tone as holiday subdues Europe grains.

text.p: A holiday on Thursday in several countries and no EU grain tender this week or next, meant the weather has reigned supreme in Europe's cereals markets.
And as the weekend approached, forecast rains were eagerly awaited.
The next EU grain tender will be held on May 15. And the 15 ECUs a tonne tax imposed on EU daily wheat exports has helped to stifle exporting.
Weather continued to dominate French grain trade this week, after last weekend's rainy spell forced down wheat, barley and maize prices.
But business was very slow due to the May 1 public holiday.
"The lack of players keeps trade at a standstill. The weather is the main focus," one dealer said.

A rainy front hit France last weekend, bringing some relief to thirsty crops and pushing new-crop prices down. Dry and warm weather returned on Wednesday but prices remained under pressure as forecasters predicted more rain over the coming weekend.
"Everyone is waiting to see if the new rain will bring some relief to the crops," one dealer said.
Farmers are anxiously monitoring weather forecasts as lasting rain is badly needed to help solve problems caused by the prolonged drought.
Lack of export prospects also kept old crop wheat under pressure.
Germany also took Thursday's holiday, and trading was featureless Friday.
"I'm keeping business to a minimum today because there aren't any fresh factors in the market and there is hardly anyone to talk to," an export trader in Hamburg said.
Further west prices were expected to fall as favourable rains were helping to ease the damaging effects of drought but German prices should withstand the price pressure for longer, traders said.
Wheat sellers expected western European countries to need German supplies, because of harvest losses in the higher quality grades.
They also placed their hopes on eastern European demand.
Old crop barley and rye on the open market are now scarce because they have been mostly absorbed by feed compounders and intervention stores.
British traders are also watching the weather closely. They had no holiday on Thursday, but there is one on Monday and the election combined with the weather to create a nervous, subdued market.
"It's a bit of a nervous market," one trader said. "We're trading weather, we've been trading the election and we're trading sterling," he said.

Sterling's immediate post-election slide tempted out some interest from other European destinations in UK grain, but the UK currency soon recovered much of its losses and any advantage was likely to be shortlived, traders said.
It was not clear whether new rain predicted at the weekend would push down prices. "It has to convince the bulls in the market that it's doing some good," the trader said.
By Friday, trade was "more about pre-holiday book squaring," than more fundamental factors, he said.
Italian wheat prices continued to move higher driven by the upward trend to international grain markets and a rise in domestic demand while producers were reluctant to sell.

The market is still concerned over dry weather. Although recent rain has helped, this is not seen enough for crops to recover fully from the dry spell that has lasted through late winter and early spring.

Heavy rainstorms through northern Italy last week at the weekend (Sunday April 27) have helped lessen the effect of months of drought, but traders say further rain across the whole nation is needed for crops to fully recovery.
Spanish grains prices were largely static on Wednesday, after which a natinonal holiday on Thursday and a local holiday in Madrid on Monday stifled trade.
Barley prices in the north weakened on prospects of a good local harvest, dealers said.
Fears over the spread of the outbreak of swine fever in the Catalan province of Lerida have yet to influence feed prices because farmers continue to hoard stocks, a local dealer said.
"In the province there's a good harvest forecast, but the big question remains as to how much of last year's barley is left over," he said.
He estimated that as much as two million tonnes of barley could still be being kept back by suppliers, and forecast this year's harvest at around 7.5 million tonnes.
"That total is bigger than what Spain consumes, so these figures should weigh on prices eventually."
Fears of increasing incidents of swine fever in the region were based on the fact that few official data have been supplied, he added.
"It's clear that they're trying to play it down because they don't want to start a scare".
"It could affect the grains market a lot. I've heard talk of up to 800,000 pigs being killed. But it's all a bit cloudy at the moment," he added.
Other cereal prices were little changed, with prospects for this year's harvest less optimistic after a spate of dry weather.
"We're expecting the wheat harvest to be around 10-15 percent lower than last year," said a Madrid dealer.
Last year Spain produced 6 million tonnes of wheat, official data show.
Prospects for maize were better however, as it is only just being sown and therefore the dry weather has not affected it.
"In any case maize is a irrigated crop, so it's more resistant," the Madrid dealer added.
The weather is expected to be warm and sunny over most of the country until Saturday, with some scattered rain in the northwest over the weekend.
